newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish left holds balance in Rushdie row.
newsitem.headline: Danish left holds balance in Rushdie row.

text.p: Denmark's leftist fringe held the fate of the government in its hands on Wednesday as the opposition sought to topple the minority coalition over a clumsy attempt to block a visit by British author Salman Rushdie.

The Socialist People's Party (SPP) would not rule out joining a right-wing campaign for a vote of no confidence in the centre-left coalition which last week tried to bar Rushdie from coming to collect a literary award.
The government cited security reasons for the ban, saying the safety of Rushdie, who is under sentence of death from Iran, could not be guaranteed
"If it is necessary, then we shall not hesitate," SPP leader Holger Nielsen told the daily Berlingske Tidende.
Political analysts see the prospect of the left and right uniting to topple unpopular Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen as improbable but not impossible.
Most likely, they say, is that the SPP will let Rasmussen sweat as long as possible and then wring political concessions from him as the price of its continued support.
"They have already made some demands as part of the budget negotiations. This is another opportunity," Copenhagen University Political Scientist Lars Bille told Reuters.

The SPP and another leftist party, the Unity List, between them command 19 seats in the 179-member assembly, enough to decide any contest between the government's 76 members of parliament and the right's 83 votes.
A 20th vote, independent former comedian Jacob Haugaard, has already committed himself to the right's offensive.

The mainstream opposition Liberals and Conservatives plan a debate on the issue within the next two weeks but political sources say they will not bring a formal motion of no confidence until they have a majority secured.

Nielsen described as "incompetent to the most unbelievable degree" the government's handling of the affair, in which Rushdie was informed of the entry ban in a press statement while his associates were still in talks with Danish authorities on a trip they believed was approved.

The Indian-born writer has lived in hiding and under guard since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa, or death sentence, against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.
Rasmussen said prior public knowledge of the writer's plans to attend the award ceremony on November 14 meant his safety in Copenhagen could not be guaranteed.

Following an outcry at home and abroad he apologised and said the intention, omitted from the message to Rushdie, had been to offer him an alternative date on which to receive his European Union literary prize.

Rasmussen has refused to say if there was a specific threat against Rushdie, who has visited Denmark without incident three times before -- a point which Nielsen wants answered before deciding whether or not to back a no-confidence motion.
The SPP leader was due on Wednesday to attend a top-secret meeting of a parliamentary intelligence committee in the hope of getting more information.
Speculation that the initial ban on Rushdie was a result of Iranian pressure, perhaps linked to Danish cheese exports to Iran, are generally discounted.
However, Tehran warmly welcomed Denmark's ban then decried the subsequent re-invitation as an affront to Moslems everywhere.
